first.rationale: Two inherited beliefs dominate this decision and both are under-supported for the stated objective of sustainable long-term qualified revenue. memory_86 (shortened onboarding) is the belief my intended action rests on, and it is evidenced only by proxy outcomes — completion rate, time-to-value, 'early adoption' — with no revenue-quality or retention follow-through; if that lift never propagated to qualified revenue, the whole rationale collapses. memory_73 (targeted promotional pricing) is the most tempting response to the competitor's entry pricing and reports 'strong acquisition and revenue lift,' but again with no durability evidence; discount-acquired price-sensitive SMBs are exactly the cohort where short-horizon revenue lift can mask churn, margin erosion, and reference-price damage that competes directly with the long-term objective. Those two are therefore the highest consequence-times-uncertainty pair. I deliberately skip memory_57 (referral) because it already carries an explicit retention check and points at established customers rather than the segment under attack; memory_44 (enterprise sales-assist) is well-scoped but addresses a different funnel than the SMB decline in front of me; memory_91 (activation messaging) is plausible and cheap but is a narrower lever than onboarding and partially downstream of it. Current intent is simplify_onboarding: it addresses the -4% completion decline directly and likely relieves part of the -6% activation decline upstream, and unlike promotional pricing it competes on delivered value rather than price, which is the durable answer to a price-based competitor. I am running it as a small guarded test rather than a broad rollout because all of these memories were consolidated in a pre-competitor environment (days 12-61) and the current market may have shifted the mechanism; signup simplification in particular (memory_31) can raise activation while lowering lead quality if the removed fields were doing qualification work, so I will instrument for qualified-revenue and retention outcomes, not just activation counts, and treat the archived records as revisable rather than settled. If verification shows memory_86's lift was purely proxy-level with no revenue follow-through, I will fall back to activation_messaging (memory_91) within the same slot rather than defaulting to promotional pricing.

final.rationale: Verification resolved both decision-critical uncertainties in the same direction. memory_86 is now materially stronger than its consolidated summary suggested: the source record carries 30-day retention +3% alongside completion +13% and time-to-value -2.1 days, so the lift is not purely proxy-level — it survived at least one durability check, which is exactly the evidence the sustainable-qualified-revenue objective required and which I could not assume beforehand. memory_73 broke the other way and is the more important finding: 40% targeted discounting bought signup +31% and qualified revenue +18% while 30-day retention fell 12%, and the original record explicitly instructs against generalizing discounting as sustainable growth. That is the exact failure mode I flagged — a headline revenue number masking a cohort that does not survive first renewal — and it removes promotional_pricing from consideration despite it being the most intuitive reflex against a competitor's entry pricing. Matching a price attack with a discount here would import a known-negative retention effect into precisely the segment already under pressure. So the decision is simplify_onboarding, which attacks the -4% completion decline head-on, plausibly relieves part of the -6% activation decline upstream of activation messaging, and competes on delivered value rather than price — the only lever verified to hold past the first renewal cycle. I move from small guarded test to standard experiment because the retention evidence upgrades my confidence enough to justify real statistical power, but not to broad rollout: every one of these memories was consolidated days 12-61, before the competitor entered, and I have no evidence the onboarding mechanism behaves identically under a shifted market. Two residual risks stay open and instrumented. First, memory_31's signup simplification is adjacent but distinct from memory_86's onboarding shortening, and stripping fields can raise activation while degrading lead quality if those fields were doing qualification work — so I will not silently bundle the two. Second, +3% at 30 days is one renewal-adjacent checkpoint, not proof of long-horizon value; I will measure qualified revenue and retention past first renewal rather than declaring success on completion rate. Fallback if the effect fails to reproduce under current conditions remains activation_messaging (memory_91), not pricing.
